Set. The god of chaos, desert, and violence. He murdered his brother Osiris in a power struggle but was ultimately defeated by Osiris's son Horus. Despite his chaotic nature, Set was not purely evil in Egyptian belief but rather represented the necessary wild forces that needed containment within the ordered cosmos. Red-haired and depicted with a strange composite animal head, possibly an aardvark or donkey, Set symbolized his otherness and chaos. He sparked the central conflict of Egyptian mythology by murdering his brother Osiris, drowning him and then tearing him to pieces in his lust for power. He was defeated in combat by Horus, who claimed his father's throne and the kingdom of Egypt. Set was the god of the desert, storms, and foreign lands, representing the untamed forces outside the Nile Valley's ordered civilization. But he was also invoked as a protector against chaos and disease, wielding destructive power for beneficial purposes when needed. Paradoxically, Set was associated with the chaos serpent Apophis and the battles against Ra, sometimes even depicted fighting the chaos serpent himself. Despite his villainy in the Osiris myth, Set maintained a place in the divine pantheon and was worshipped, especially in Avaris in the Delta. He embodied the principle that chaos and order must coexist. The Egyptian cosmos required both. The struggle between Set and Horus was not merely a tale of good defeating evil, but a cosmic principle about the eternal tension between order and disorder. This balance was essential to the universe's continuation.
